On July, 29,1958, he opposed the direction of <NAME> for writing to <NAME> to deposit the securities in the <ORG> as that would entail heavy withdrawal charges in case the sale and purchase of securities were not to be stopped while, according to his statement the next day, he himself suggested to <NAME> in August, 1955, that <NAME> be asked to deposit all the securities in the <ORG> or to send them to the head office. He denied the suggestion that he made this change in his statement under pressure of the <ORG>. The cross-examination was really directed to show that he had been approached by the police between the close of his examination on July 29 and his further examination on July 30, 1958. <NAME> admitted in court that after giving evidence he went to the room allotted in the Court building to <ORG> and that the Investigating Officer and the Secretary to the Administrator of the Insurance Company were there. He went there in order to take certain papers which he had kept there. He, however, had not brought any papers on July 30 as, accord- 325 ing to him, his main cross-examination had been over. He however denied that he had been dictated notes by the police in order to answer questions in cross-examination or that be remained with the police till 9 p. m. or that the Secretary to the Administrator held out a threat about the forfeiture of his gratuity in case be did not make a statement favourable to the prosecution. We see no Reason for the police to bring pressure on <NAME> to introduce falsely the conversation in August. Between July 14, 1955, and middle of August, 1955, the head office learnt of the purchase of securities of the face value of Rs. 74,00,000 and again, on or about August 26, of the purchase of securities of the face value of Rs. 40,00,000. A further conversation in August is therefore most likely as deposed to. The main fact remains that <NAME> said that the securities be sent for in December, 1955, which implies his knowledge of the transactions in question. We are of opinion that the discrepancies or contradictions pointed out in <NAME> statement are not such as to discredit him and make him an unreliable witness and that he is not shown to be under the influence of the prosecution. Further, his various statements connecting <NAME> with the crime, find corroboration from other evidence. Letter Exhibit P. 1351 dated September 4, 1954, was sent to <ORG>, Delhi Branch, under the signature of <NAME> as Chairman. The letter directed the bank to deliver certain securities to the bearer. <NAME> admits his signatures on this document and also on the letter Exhibit P. 1352 acknowledging the receipt of the securities sent for, thus corroborating <NAME> statement that the securities were withdrawn under his instructions. 326 Letters Exhibit D. 3, dated March 16, 1955, and P. 892 dated August 5, 1955, from <NAME> to <NAME>, mentioned that the stock certificates were being sent under the instructions of the Chairman. They corroborate <NAME>'s statements in <ORG> of the dispatch of these stock certificates under <NAME>'s instructions. He had no reason to use this expression if he was sending them on his own. It is true that the date on which the Chairman gave the instruction is not proved, but it stands to reason that the stock certificates must have been despatched soon after the receipt of the instruction from the Chairman. it cannot be presumed that in such transactions there could be such delay as would make statement in these letters not corroborative evidence under s. 157 , of the Evidence Act which provides that previous statements made at or about the time a fact took place can be used for corroborating the statement in <ORG>. <NAME>'s statement that he did not mention the name of <ORG> in his letters to the head office as be did not want <ORG> to know about the dealings with <ORG>, implies that in the ordinary course of business the information conveyed in those letters would be communicated to <ORG> and thus tends to support <NAME> statement that he used to visit <ORG> on receipt of the statement of account and inform him about the purchase or sale of the securities. <NAME> had been inconsistent about <NAME> later knowledge of the existence of <ORG>. In answer to question No. 66, on November 13, 1958, he stated : "I did not contradict the statement made in Ex xi :P. 813 that cheque No. B564809 dated 17-11-54 had been issued in favour of <NAME> although that cheque had in fact been issued in favour of <ORG> and not in favour of <NAME> because those at the Head Office did not know anything about <ORG>". In answer to question No. 149, on November 14, 1958, he stated: "I did not mention the name of <ORG> in my letters addressed to <ORG> as the party with whom there were cross contracts because <NAME> would not have known as to what was <ORG>. I also did not mention the name of <ORG> in my letters to <ORG> because I did not want <NAME> to know that I was having dealings with <ORG>. I also want to add that <NAME> must have known that the cross-contracts were with <ORG> because the name of <ORG> was mentioned as the payee on the counterfoils of the cheques issued in favour of <ORG>." <NAME> seems to have attempted to undo the effect of his statement on November 13, but being of divided mind, made inconsistent statements even on November 14, 1958. He was in difficult position. He attempted to show that <ORG> did not know about <ORG> and also to show that <NAME> had reasons to know about it and was therefore in the position of an Accomplice, a stand which is also taken by <ORG> We may now deal first with the case of <NAME>, appellant. <NAME> has admitted his entering into the various transactions of purchase and sale and to have set up <ORG> for convenience to carry out the scheme of diverting the funds of <ORG> to the Union Agencies by way of temporary loan. His main plea is that he had no attention to cause loss to <ORG> and did not know that the way he arranged funds for the Union Agencies from <ORG> was against law. He contends that he had no dishonest intentions and therefore did not commit any of the offences he had been charged with, and convicted of. Learned counsel for <ORG> has urged two points in addition to some of the points of law urged by learned counsel for <ORG>. He urged that the transactions entered into by <ORG> were ordinary genuine commercial transactions and that there was no evidence of <ORG>'s acting dishonestly in entering into those transactions. It is further said that <ORG> recorded no finding, on the latter point though it was necessary to record such a finding, even though this point was not seriously urged. In support of the contention that the purchase and sale transactions were genuine commercial transactions, it is urged that to meet the losses of <ORG> <ORG> was in a position to sell the shares held by it or could have raised the money on its credit. He did not sell the shares as they were valuable and as their sale would have affected the credit of <ORG>. <ORG> had been instructed in September, 1954, that the yield from the investment of <ORG> was not good and that the funds of <ORG> be invested in securities. Such instructions are said to have been given when he was authorised by <ORG> to purchase and sell securities on behalf of <ORG>. It is suggested that these instructions were given in 1953 and not in 1954 when <ORG> was going abroad. In view of this authority, <ORG> decided on a course of action by which he could invest the insurance money in securities and also help <ORG>. It is submitted that it was not necessary to mention <ORG> to the head office as <ORG> was going to suffer no loss and was simply concerned in knowing of the sale and purchase transactions. <ORG>'s payment of the purchase price in anticipation of the delivery of the securities, was bona fide. We have already expressed the opinion- that the transaction in connection with the investment of the funds of <ORG> were not bonafide purchase and sale transactions. They were transactions with a purpose. They were motivated in the interests of the Union Agencies and not in the interests of <ORG>. - The mere fact that on account of the nondelivery of securities within a reasonable time of the payment of the purchase money made the brokers or <ORG> or both of them liable to an action, does not change the nature of the transactions. That liability can co-exist with the criminal liability of <NAME> if the transactions were such which could amount to his committing breach of trust. In fact, the offence of breach of trust is not with respect to his entering into the sale and purchase transactions. It is really on the basis of his paying the money out of the Insurance Company's funds to the Union Agencies through <ORG>, in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money. These purchase and sale transactions were just a device for drawing on those funds. <ORG> came into existence just when the Union Agencies suffered losses and was not in a position to pay them and, consequently, there arose the necessity for <ORG> and <ORG> to devise means to raise funds for meeting those losses. <NAME> opened the banking accounts in two banks at Bombay on August 9 and August 11, 1954, depositing the two sums of Rs. 1,100 each in each of the two banks. He states that he got this money from <NAME>. The money was, however withdrawn after a short time and paid back to <ORG> and no further contribution to the funds of the <ORG> was made on his behalf. The Company functioned mainly on the amounts received from <ORG>. <NAME>, therefore, cannot be said to be quite innocent of the starting of the company and the nature of its business. He started, in answer to question No. 24: "I started business in the name of <ORG> in 1953, or beginning of 1954. 1 however did no business in the name of that company. <NAME> stated that I should do business for the purchase or sale of securities." and in answer to question No. 26 he stated that he had no knowledge about <NAME>'s entering into contracts on behalf of <ORG> for the purchase of securities and his entering into crose-contracts with the same firm of brokers for the sale of those securities on behalf of <ORG> but admitted that he knew that <NAME> was doing business for the purchase and sale of securities on behalf of <ORG>. He expressed ignorance about similar future contracts for purchase of securities on behalf of <ORG> and cross-contracts for the sale of those securities on behalf of <ORG>. <NAME>, however, made a statement at the close of the day when he had made the above statement, and said: "In answer to question No. 24 I want to state that I did not start business of <ORG> in 1953 or the beginning of 1951 but only intended to start that business." The latter statement deserves no acceptance and is a clear indication that the implications of his earlier statement worked on his mind and he attempted to indicate that he was not even responsible in any way for the starting of the business of <ORG>. <ORG> did come into existence and ostensibly did business. The latter statement therefore cannot be true. <NAME> further knew, as his answer to question No. 157 indicates, that <ORG> did shares speculation business at Bombay. He, however, stated that he did not know on behalf of which company he did that business. What <NAME> actually did in connection with the various transactions which helped in the diversion of the funds of <ORG> to <ORG> has to be looked at in this background. He cashed a number of cheques issued on behalf of <ORG> and made over that money to <ORG>, who passed it on the <ORG>. Agencies. He issued cheques on behalf of <ORG> in favour of Bharat <ORG> Agencies after the amounts of the cheques of <ORG> in favour of <ORG> had been deposited in the Bank. Some of these cheques issued in favour of <ORG> Agencies were filled in by <NAME> himself and therefore he must have known that he was passing on the money to <ORG>. In fact, some of the cheques issued on behalf of <ORG> in favour of <ORG> were deposited in the bank by <NAME> himself It is therefore not possible to believe that <NAME> did not know that the amounts which his company viz., <ORG>, received from <ORG> must have purported to be on account of securities sold to <ORG>, as that was the business which <ORG> professed to do and, according to him, he knew to be its business, He knew that most of this amount was passed on to <ORG>. Both these facts must have put him on enquiry even if he did not initially know of the nature of the business which brought in the money to, and took out the money from, <ORG>. He is expected to knew that <ORG> was not likely to purchase securities so frequently. If he had made enquiries, he would have learnt about the nature of receipts and payments and in fact we are inclined to the view that he must have known of their nature and that it is not reasonable that he would be completely in the dark. The business of <ORG> is said to have been started as <NAME> was not taking interest in the other business. This should indicate that he must have evinced interest in the activities of <ORG> which continued for over a year and which made him receive and dispose of lakhs of Rupees. Surely, it is not expected that he would have made no effort to know what is required to be know by one earring on business for the purchase and sale of securities, and any attempt to have known this would have necessarily led him to know that securities were being purchased on behalf of <ORG> and were not delivered to it and that <ORG> purchased no securities from <ORG> and that any payment by it to the latter was for something which <ORG> was not liable to pay. It follows that he must have known that money was being received from <ORG> for nothing which was due to <ORG> from that company and that most of that money was being paid to <ORG> for payment of which <ORG> had no liability and that the net result of the transactions of receipt of money from <ORG> and payment of it to <ORG> was that <ORG> was acting to help the diversion of funds from <ORG> to <ORG>. We therefore hold that <NAME> has been rightly found to be in the conspiracy. We may now deal with the case of <ORG>, appellants The fact that the funds of <ORG> were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved by the prosecution, is not challenged by <ORG>. His main contention is that he did not know what <NAME> had been doing in connection with the raising of funds for meeting the losses of the Union Agencies. There is, however, ample evidence to indicate that <ORG> knew of the scheme of the transactions and was a party to the scheme inasmuch as the transactions were carried through under his instructions and approval: The facts which have a bearing on this matter are: (1) Dalmia had the clearest motive to devise means for meeting the losses of the Union Agencies. 337 (2) <NAME> actually looked after the share business of <ORG> at Calcutta and Delhi. He had knowledge of the losses of <ORG>. (3) The frequency of telephonic calls between him and <NAME> during the period when the losses took place and steps were taken to meet them, especially during the early stages in August and September, 1954, when the scheme was being put into operation, and in July and August, 1955, when there bad been heavy and recurring losses. (4) <NAME>'s informing <ORG>, Delhi, on September 4, 1954, about his powers to deal with securities and actually withdrawing securities that- day, which were shortly after sold at Bombay and whose proceeds were utilised for meeting the losses. (5) The gradually increasing retention of securities in the office of <ORG> and consequently the gradually reduced deposit of securities in the Banks. (6) The transfer of securities held by <ORG> from Delhi to Bombay when funds were low there to meet the losses. (7) The purchase and sale of securities in the relevant period in order to meet the losses were under his instructions. (8) A larger use of converting securities into inscribed stock certificates which was used for concealing the disclosure of the interval between the date of purchase of the securities which were then not received, and the date when those securities were recouped later. (9) <NAME>'s annoyance and resentment on September 9, 1955, when the auditors made a surprise inspection of the office of the insurance company and wanted to see the securities, (10) His conduct on September 15, 1955. (11) His not going to meet Mr. <NAME> on September 16, 1955, and instead, sending his relatives to state what was not the full and correct statement of facts which, according to his own statements, were known to him by then. (12) His confession P. 10 together with the statement Exhibit p. 11 and the statement made to Annadhanam that he carried on his speculative business in shares in the name of <ORG>. One of the main factors urged in support of the contention that <NAME> was in the conspiracy is that the entire scheme of conspiracy was entered into for the sole benefit of <NAME>. It is not reasonably probable that such a conspiracy would come into existence without the knowledge or consent of <NAME>. The conspiracy charge framed against <NAME> mentioned the object of the conspiracy as 'meeting losses, suffered by you, R. <NAME>, in forward transactions, of speculation in shares, which transactions were carried on in the name of <ORG>...' and the charge under s. 409  1 . P. C. referred to the dishonest utilisation of the funds of <ORG>. This matter has been considered from several aspects. The first in that <NAME> is said to have owned the entire shares issued by <ORG>, or at least to have owned a substantial part of them and was in a position to control the other shareholders. To appreciate this aspect, it is necessary to give an account of the share-holding in this company. <ORG> was incorporated at Bombay on April 1, 1948, as a private limited company, with its registered office at Bombay. It also had an office at 10, Daryaganj, Delhi, where the head office of <ORG> was. Its authorised capital was Rs. 5,00,000. The total number of shares issued in 1949 Was 2,000, Out of these <NAME> held 1,200 shares, <NAME> Cement & Paper Marketing Company Ltd. (hereinafter called <ORG>) 600 shares, <NAME>, brother of <NAME>, 100 shares and <NAME>, the balance of 100 shares. The same position of share-holding continued in 1950. In 1951, <NAME> continued to hold 1,200 shares, but the other 800 shares were hold by <ORG>. The position continued in 1952 as well and, in the first half of 1953, <NAME> increased the number of his shares to 1,800 and <ORG> increased theirs to 1,200 and the total shares issued thus stood at 3,000. This position continued up to September 21, 1954. On September 22, 1954, 2,000 shares were further issued to <NAME>, a nominee of <ORG>. The total shares on that date stood at 5,000 of which <ORG> held 1,800, <ORG> 1,200, and <ORG> 2,000. On October 4, 1954, <NAME> and <NAME> each got 100 shares from <ORG> with the result that thereafter the position of shareholding was: <ORG> 1,800; <ORG> 1000; <ORG> 2,000; <ORG> 10); and <ORG> 100, out of the total number of issued shares of 5000. It is said that <ORG> transferred his 1,800 ,shares to one <NAME> on October 30, 1954. <NAME>'s holding 1,800 shares was mentioned in the return, Exhibit P. 3122 filed by <ORG> as regards share capital and shares as on December 31, 1955, in the office of the Register of Companies in January 1956 with respect to the year 1955. The return showed that the transfer had taken place on January 31, 1955. It would appear that the alleged sale of shares to <NAME> in October 1954 was not mentioned in a similar return which must have been submitted to the Registrar of Companies in January, 1955, and that therefore its transfer was show on January 31, 1955, Probably a date subsequent to the submission of the relevant return for the year 1954. A brief account of the various share-holders may be given. <NAME> was a Director of <ORG>, and was succeeded, on his resignation, by <NAME>, who was an Accountant in <ORG>. He was also an employee of another company named <ORG> Another Director of <ORG> was <NAME>, lncome-tax Adviser in the concerns of <NAME>. The share scrips in <ORG> standing in the name of <ORG> and three blank share transfer forms signed by <NAME> as Secretary of <ORG>, in the column entitled 'seller' were recovered from <NAME>'s house on search on November 25, 1955. <NAME> was the personal accountant of <NAME> and Manager of <ORG>. The inference drawn by the <ORG> below from these circumstances is that <ORG> was the concern of <NAME>, and this is reasonable. No Satisfactory explanation is given why the shares standing in the name of <ORG> and the blank transfer forms should be found in <NAME>'s residence. <NAME> was the personal accountant of <ORG> and Manager of the Delhi <ORG>, and was also Secretary of <ORG> <ORG> appears to be a sister concern of <ORG>. It was previously known as <ORG> Jain Aviation Ltd. It installed a telephone at one of <ORG>'s residences in January, 1953. Its offices were in the same room in which the offices of <ORG> were. <NAME>, who succeeded <ORG> as Director of <ORG>, was an employee of <ORG>. <NAME> was the Accountant of <ORG>, in addition to being Director of <ORG>. He bad powers over the staff of both the companies. <NAME> was Director of <ORG> and held 100 shares in <ORG> as nominee of <ORG>, from October 4, 1954, and 1,000 shares as nominee of <ORG>, from some time about January 31, 1955. <NAME>, <NAME> and G. L. <ORG>, were authorised to operate on the account of both <ORG>, Calcutta, and <ORG>, with <ORG>, Calcutta. The issue and transfer of shares of <ORG> in September and October, 1954, seem to be in pursuance of an attempt to meet a contention, as at present urged for the <ORG>, that <ORG> was the largest shareholder in it. The same idea seemed to have led to the transfer of shares to <ORG> by <ORG>. The verbal assertion of the sale having taken place in October, 1954, is not supported by the entry in Exhibit P. 3122 and what may be taken to be the entries in a similar return for the year 1954. This can go to support the allegation that <ORG> knew about the shady transactions which were in progress from early August, 1954. The learned Sessions Judge relied on the following circumstances for his conclusion that <ORG> was synonymous with <ORG>. "1. The speculation business of <ORG>, the paid up capital of which nearly all belonged to <ORG> was on the liquidation of that company taken over by <ORG> and more or less the same persons conducted the business of <ORG> who were previously looking after <ORG> Cement & Paper Marketing Company. 2. <ORG> was known and taken to be the concern of Dalmia by its then Accountant <NAME> and by the brokers with whom it had dealings 3. <NAME>, who hold power of attorney on behalf of <ORG> and <ORG>, told the brokers at the time he gave business of <ORG> to them J. that it was the business of <ORG>. 4. The salaries of personal and domestic employees of <ORG> were paid by <ORG> and those payments were debited to the Salaries Account of the company. The personal employees of <ORG> were thus treated as the employees of <ORG>. 5. The business done in the name of <ORG> with <NAME> was treated as the business of <ORG>. 6. The funds of <ORG> were used to discharge an obligation personally undertaken by <ORG>. The price of the shares purchased in the process in the name of <ORG> was paid out of the funds of <ORG> and the purchase of those shares was treated in the books of <ORG> as part of its investment. 7. When sister-in-law of <NAME> wanted money it was lent to her out of the funds of <ORG> and in the books of that company no interest was charged from her". It has been strenuously urged by Mr. <NAME> that what certain persons considered to be the nature of <ORG> or what <NAME> told them could not be evidence against <NAME> with respect to the question whether he could be said to be identical with <ORG>. We need not consider this legal objection as it is not very necessary to rely on these considerations for the purpose of the finding on this point. It may be said, however, that prima facie there seems to be no legal bar to the admissibility of statements that <NAME> told certain persons that <ORG> was the business of <NAME>. He had authority to represent <NAME> and <ORG> on the basis of the power of attorney held by him from both. His statement would thus appear to be the statement of their 'agent' in the course of the business. We have considered the reasons given for the other findings by the learned Sessions Judge and accepted by <ORG> and are of opinion that the findings are correct and that they can lead to no other conclusion than that no distinction existed between <NAME> and <ORG> and that whenever it suited <NAME> or the interests of <ORG> such transactions of one could be changed to those on behalf of the other. We may, however, refer to one matter. <NAME> admits having purchased shares of <NAME> Jain Airways of the face value of Rs.6,00,000/from <NAME>, on behalf of <ORG>, in his own name, though the real purchaser was <ORG> and that he did so as the seller and his solicitor did not agree to sell the shares in the name of the latter. The explanation does not appear to be satisfactory. The seller had no interest in whose name the sale took place so long as he gets the money for the shares he was selling. Mr. <NAME> has urged that these various considerations may indicate strong association of <NAME> with <ORG> but are not sufficient to establish his complete identity with it, as is necessary to establish in view of the charges framed. <NAME>'s identity with <ORG> or having great interest in it is really a matter providing motive for <NAME>'s going to the length of entering into a conspiracy to raise funds for Meeting the losses of <ORG> by diverting the funds of <ORG> and which would amount to Committing criminal breach of trust. <NAME> admits having given instructions about the business of <ORG> in 1954 when he was not a Director of that company, and in 1955 when he was not even a shareholder. <NAME>'s own statement to <ORG> on September 20, 1955, goes to support the conclusion in this respect. He stated to him then that he had lost the moneys in speculation which he did through his private companies and that most of those transactions were through <ORG>. Further, the charge said that he committed criminal breach of trust of the funds of <ORG> by wilfully suffering <NAME> to dishonestly misappropriate them and dishonestly use them or dispose of them in violation of the directions of law and the implied contract existing between <NAME> and <ORG> prescribing the mode in which such trust was to be discharged. It was in describing the manner of the alleged dishonest misappropriation or the use or disposal of the said funds in violation of the legal and contractual directions that the charge under s. 409 I.P.C. described the Manner to consist of withdrawing the funds from the banks by cheques in favour of <ORG> and by the utilisation of those funds for meeting losses' suffered by <NAME> in forward transactions in shares carried on in the name of <ORG>, and for other purposes not connected with the affairs of <ORG>. Even in this description of the manner, the emphasis ought to be placed on the expression 'for meeting losses suffered by <NAME> in forward transactions in shares carried on in the name of the <ORG> and for other purposes not connected with the affairs of the said <ORG>' and not on the alleged losses suffered by <NAME> personally. We are therefore of opinion that firstly the evidence is adequate to establish that <NAME> and <ORG> can be said to be interchangeable and, secondly, that even if that is not possible to say, <NAME> had sufficient motive, on account of his intimate relations with <ORG>, for committing breach of trust, and thirdly, that the second finding does not in any way adversely affect the establishment of the offence under s. 409 I. P. C. against <NAME> even though the charge described the utilisation of the money in a somewhat different manner. The entire scheme of the transactions must start at the instance of the person or persons who were likely to suffer in case the losses of <ORG> were not paid at the proper time. There is no doubt that in the first instance it would be <ORG> as a company which would suffer in its credit and its activities. We have found that <NAME> was so intimately connected with this com- pany as could make him a sort of a sole proprietor of the company. He was to lose immensely in case the credit of <ORG> suffered, as it was commonly believed to be his concern and he bad connections and control over a number of business concerns and had a high stake in the business world. His prestige and credit were bound to suffer severely as a result of <ORG> losing credit in the market. There is evidence on record that if the losses are not promptly paid, the defaulter would suffer in credit and may not be able to persuade the brokers to enter into contracts with him. It is suggested for <ORG> that <NAME> had a greater interest in seeing that <ORG> does not suffer in credit. We do not agree. If the <ORG> failed on account of its losing credit in the market on its failure to meet the losses, <NAME> may stand to lose his service with the <ORG>. That would have meant the loss of a few hundred rupees a month. In fact, he need not have suffered any loss. He could have been employed by <ORG> who bad great confidence in him and whom he had been serving faithfully for a long time. <NAME>, as agent of <ORG>, had certainly credit in the market. There is evidence of his good reputation, but much of it must have been the result of his association with <ORG> and his concerns. He really enjoyed reflected glory. He bad no personal interest in the matter as <ORG> had. We therefore do not consider this suggestion to be sound and are of opinion that <ORG> was the only person who bad to devise means to meet the losses of the <ORG>. Further, <ORG> admits that he used to give instructions with regard to the speculation-in-shares business of the <ORG> at Calcutta and Delhi during 1954 and 1955, and stated, in answer to question No. 210 with respect to the evidence that Delhi Office of the <ORG> used to supply funds for meeting the losses suffered by it in the speculation business at Calcutta and Delhi: "'It is correct that as the result of shares speculation business at Calcutta and <ORG> suffered losses in the final analysis. I was once told by <NAME> on telephone from Calcutta that <NAME> had informed him that <ORG> would arrange for funds for the losses suffered by <ORG>. It was within my knowledge that if <ORG> of the Bharat Union Agencies was not in a position to supply full funds for meeting the losses at Calcutta <ORG> would supply those funds." And, in answer to question No. 211 which referred to the evidence about <ORG> being short of liquid funds from August, 1954, onwards and in 1955, to meet the losses, he said "It was within my knowledge that <ORG> was holding very large number of shares. But I did not know the name of the Companies of which the shares were held by the <ORG> and the quantum of those shares." <NAME> also admitted his knowledge that <NAME> had entered into contract for the forward sale of <ORG> Shares at Bombay on behalf of <ORG> during 1954 and 1955 and that <ORG> suffered losses on this business, but stated that he did not know the extent or details of the losses. <NAME> must be expected not only to know the losses which <ORG> suffered, but also their extent. He is also expected to devise or at least know the ways in which those losses would be met. A mere vague knowledge, as stated, about <ORG> possessing a number of shares could not have been sufficient satisfaction about the losses being successfully met. It is to be noted that he did not deny that <ORG> was short of funds and that it used to supply funds to meet the losses. Further, if <NAME>'s statement about <ORG>'s communication to him be correct, it would appear that when the Bombay Office of <ORG> was not in a position to meet the losses, <NAME> would not think of arranging, on his own, funds to meet the losses, but would first approach <ORG> of <ORG>. <ORG>, then, if unable to meet the losses, would necessarily obtain instructions from <NAME>. It can therefore be legitimately concluded that <NAME> alone, or in consultation with <NAME>, devised the scheme of the transactions which led to the diversion of the funds. of <ORG> to <ORG> and carried it out with the help of the other appellants. It has been contended both for <ORG> and for <ORG> that funds could have been found to meet the losses of <ORG> by means other than the diversion of the Insurance Company's funds. We need not discuss whether the shares held by <ORG> at the time could be sold to raise the funds or whether on the mere credit of <ORG> funds could be raised in no time. These courses were not adopted. The selling of the shares which <ORG> possessed, might itself affect its credit, and that no business concern desires, especially a concern dealing in sharespeculation business. <ORG> had been in telephonic communication with <NAME>. It is significant, even though there is no evidence about the content of the conversations, that there had been frequent calls, during the period of the losses in August and September, 1954, between <ORG>'s telephone and that of <NAME> at Bombay. That was the period when <ORG> was confronted with the position of arranging sufficient funds at Bombay for the purpose of diverting them to the Union Agencies. Very heavy losses were suffered in July and August, 1955. Securities of the face value of Rs. 79,00,000 and Rs. 60,00,000 were purchased in July and August, 1955, respectively. A very large number of telephone calls took place during that period between <ORG> at Delhi and <NAME> at Bombay. It is true that during certain periods of losses, the record of telephonic communications does not indicate that any telephonic communication took place. We have already stated, in considering the transactions, that the pattern of action to be taken had been fully determined by the course adopted in the first few transactions. 349 <NAME> acted according to that pattern. The only thing that he had to do in connection with further contingencies of demands for losses, was to send for securities from Delhi when the funds at Bombay were low. Such requests for the transfer of securities could be made in good time or by telephonic communication or even by letters addressed to <NAME> personally. The fact remains that a number of securities were sent from Delhi to Bombay under the directions of <NAME> when there was no apparent reason to send them other than the need to meet losses incurred or expected. <ORG> informed <ORG> at Delhi about his power to deal with securities on September 4, 1954, though he had that power from September, 1951, itself. This was at the early stage of the commencement of the losses of the Union Agencies ,suffered for a period of over a year and the planned diversion of the funds of <ORG> to meet the losses of the Union Agencies. <NAME> states that on the resignation of <NAME> it was deemed necessary that the powers of the Chairman be registered with the <ORG> so that he be in a position to operate on the securities' safecustody account of the company with the <ORG>, and that he sent the copy of the bye- laws etc., without the instructions of <NAME>, though with his knowledge, as he was told that it was necessary for the purpose of the withdrawal of the securities for which he had given instructions. This was, however, not necessary, as <NAME> bad the authority to endorse, transfer, negotiate and or deal with Government securities, etc., standing in the name of the company. We are of opinion that <NAME> took this step to enable him to withdraw the securities from the <ORG> when urgently required and another person authorised to withdraw be not available or be not prepared to withdraw them on his own. 350 The position of the securities may be brifely described on the basis of Appendix 1 of the Investigator's report Exhibit D. 74. The amount of securities at Bombay with <ORG>, on June 30, 1953, was Rs. 53,25,000 out of a total worth Rs. 2,69,57,200. The amount of securities in the <ORG> continued to be the same till March 31, 1954, even though the total amount of securities rose to Rs. 3,04,88,600. Thereafter, there had been a depletion of securities with <ORG> at Bombay with the result that on December 31, 1954, it had no securities in deposit. The amount of securities in the Imperial <ORG> of India, New Delhi, also fell subsequent to June 30, 1954. It came down to Rs. 2,60,000 on March 31, 1955, from Rs. 59,11,100 on June 30, 1954. Securities worth Rs. 52,00,000 were in the two offices on June 30, 1953. The amount of such securities kept on steadily increasing. It was Rs. 1,88,47,500 from September, 1953, to March 31, 1954. Thereafter, it rapidly increased every quarter, with the result that on March 31, 1955, the securities worth Rs. 3,76,50,804 out of the total worth Rs. 3,86,97,204 were in the offices. The overall position of the securities must have been known to <ORG>. The saving of <ORG> charges is no good explanation for keeping the securities of such a large amount, which formed a large percentage of the Company's holdings, in the offices and not in deposit with a recognized bank. The explanation seems to be that most of the securities were not really in existence. <NAME> states that be spoke to <ORG> a number of times, presumably, in July and August, 1955, about the non- receipt of the securities of the value of Rs. 81,25,000, Rs. 75,00,000 and Rs. 69,00,000 which were purchased in the months of April-May. July and August 1955 respectively, and <ORG> used to tell him that as the purchase and sale of securities had to be effected at Bombay, <ORG> could send them to the head office only after it had been decided about which securities would be finally retained by <ORG>. This statement implies that <ORG> knew and anticipated the sale of those securities and such a sale of those securities, as already mentioned, could not be in the usual course of business of the company. The securities were to be sold only if by the next due date for payment of interest they could not be recouped and did not exist with the company. Such an inference is sufficient to impute <ORG> with the knowledge of the working of the scheme. Securities were sent to Bombay from Delhi seven times during the relevant period and they were of the face value of Rs. 2,114,82,500. Securities of the face value of Rs. 17,50,000 were withdrawn from the Imperial <ORG>, Delhi, on September 4, 1954-vide Exhibit P. 1351. They were sold at Bombay on September 9, 1954. Thereafter, 30/ 1957 securities of the face value of Rs. 37,75,000 were sent on January 6, 1955. <NAME> deposes that he withdrew these from the Imperial <ORG>, Delhi, under the directions of <ORG>, and that he handed them over to <ORG>. These securites did reach Bombay. There is no clear evidence as to how they Went from Delhi to Bombay. They were sold on January 11, 1955. Eleven stock certificates of the face value of Rs. 57,72,000 were sent to Bombay on March 16, 1955, vide letter Ex. D. 3. Thereafter, stock Certificates were sent thrice in July 1955. Stock certificate in respect of 3% Bombay Loan of 1955, of the face' value of Rs. 29,75,000 was sent to Bombay on July 15, 1955-vide Exhibit P. 923. On the next day, i.e., on July 16, 1955, stock certificates of 3% Bombay Loan of 1955 of the face value of Rs. 15,50,000 and stock certificates of 3 % Loan of <ORG> of the face value of Rs. 60,500 were sent to Bombay-vide Exs. D. 1 and D. 2 respectively. J. Lastly, stock certificates of 2 3/4% Loan of 1962 of the face value of Rs. 56,00,000 were sent to Bombay on August 5, 1955. Letters Exhibits D. 3 and P. 892 state that the stock certificates mentioned therein were being sent under instructions of the Chairman'. <NAME> has deposed that the other stock certificates send with letters Exhibits D. 1, D. 2 and P. 923, were sent by him as the securities with respect to which those certificates were granted were maturing in September and were redeemable at Bombay. It has been urged that they could have been redeemed at Delhi and that they need not have been sent by <NAME> on his own a couple of months earlier. We do not consider the sending of the securities a month and a half or two months earlier than the date of maturity to be unjustified in the course of business. It is to be noticed that what was sent were the stock certificates and it might have been necessary to get the securities covered by those certificates for the purpose of redemption and that might have taken time. No pointed question was put to <NAME> as to why he sent the securities two months ahead of the date of maturity. <NAME> denies that he gave any instructions for the sending of the securities. There seems to us to be no good reason why the expression under the instructions of the Chairman' would be noted in letters Exhibits D. 3 and P. 892, unless that represented the true statement of fact. We have already discussed and expressed the opinion, in considering the evidence of <NAME>, that <NAME> was told by <NAME>, when informed of the purchase or sale of securities, that had been done under instructions and that he had confirmed them. We may further state that there is no resolution of <ORG> empowering <NAME> to deal with the Rag securities. He was, however, empowered by resolutions at the meeting of the <ORG> dated June 29, 1953, to lodge and receive G. P. Notes from <ORG> for verification and endorsement on the same and to endorse or withdraw the G. P. Notes on behalf of the company in the capacity of an agent. <NAME> was also empowered by a resolution dated October 1, 1953, to deposit and withdraw <ORG> securities held in safe custody account by the company. The aforesaid powers conferred on <NAME> are different from the powers of sale or purchase of securities. <NAME> has stated that he authorised <NAME> to purchase securities in about October, 1953,when he was to leave for abroad and that thereafter <NAME> had been purchasing and selling securities in the exercise of that authority without consulting him. It is urged for him that <NAME>'s statement that be used to obtain confirmation of the purchase and sale of the securities from him cannot be true, as there was no necessity for such confirmation. <NAME> does not appear to have exercised any such authority during the period <NAME> was abroad or till August, 1954, and therefore <NAME>'s statement does not appear to be correct. <NAME> and <NAME> were authorised to operate upon the <ORG> account at Bombay on October 1, 1953. <NAME> states, in paragraph 17 of the written statement dated March 30, 1959, that this was done as <NAME> bad been given the authority for the sale and purchase of securities at the same time. The <ORG> did not give any such authority to <NAME> and if the system of joint signatures was introduced for the reason alleged, there seems to be no good reason why the <ORG> itself did not resolve that <NAME> be empowered to sell and purchase securities. The explanation for the introduction of joint-signature scheme does not stand to reason. Even if it be not correct that <NAME> had to obtain confirmation, it stands to reason that he should report such transactions on the part of <NAME> to the Chairman, if not necessarily for his approval, at least for his information, as <NAME> had no authority to purchase and sell securities. These transactions have to be confirmed by <ORG> and therefore confirmation of the Chairman who was the only person authorised to purchase and sell securities was natural. <NAME> states that when he received no reply to his letter dated November 19, 1954, asking for distinctive numbers of securities not received at headquarters. <NAME> said that he would arrange for the dispatch of those secu- rities from Bombay to the head office. No action was apparently taken in that connection. <NAME> further states that on March 23, 1955, when he spoke to <NAME> about the non-receipt of certain securities <NAME> told him that he had already instructed <NAME> for the conversion of those securities into stock certificates and that it was in view of this statement of <NAME> that he had written letter Exhibit P. 916 to <NAME> stating therein. "You were requested for conversion of the above said G. P. Notes into Stock Certificate. The said certificate As not been received by us as yet. It may be sent now immediately as it is required for the inspection of the company's auditors. " This indicates that <NAME> was in the know of the position of securities and, on his own, gave instructions to <NAME> to convert certain securities into inscribed stock. <NAME> admits <NAME>'s speaking to him about the non- receipt of the securities and his telling him that he would ask <NAME> to send them when he would happen to talk to him on the telephone. Mention has already been made of securities of the face value of Rs. 17,50,000 being sent to Bombay from Delhi in the first week of September 1954. At the time securities of the face value of Rs.53,25,000 were in deposit in <ORG> at Bombay. There was thus no need for sending these securities from Delhi. <NAME> could have withdrawn the necessary securities from <ORG>. This indicates that on learning that there were no liquid funds for meeting the losses at Bombay, <NAME> himself decided to send these securities to Bombay for sale and for thus providing for the liquid funds there for meeting the cost of the intended fictitious purchase of securities to meet the losses of the Union Agencies. It is not suggested that these securities were sent to Bombay at the request of <NAME>. Securities withdrawn in January, 1955, and stock certificates sent in March and August, 1955, coincided with the period when <ORG> suffered losses and the funds of <ORG> at Bombay were low and were insufficient to meet the losses of <ORG>. 3% 1957 securities of the face value of Rs. 46,00,000 (Rs. 37,75,000 set from Delhi and Rs. 8,25,000 withdrawn from <ORG> at Bombay) were sold on January 11, 1955, and the proceeds were utilised in purchasing 2-3/4% 1962 securities of the face value of Rs. 46,00,000 in two lots, one of Rs. 35,00,000 and the other of Rs. 11,00,000. On January 11, 1955, Rs. 3,34,039-15-3, the balance of the sale proceeds was deposited in the accounts of <ORG>. Inscribed stock for these securities worth Rs. '46,00,000 was duly obtained. <NAME> himself handed over inscribed stock certificate to <NAME> some time in the end of January 1955. This purchase, though genuine, was not a purchase in the ordinary course of business, but was for the purpose of procuring the inscribed stock certificate to satisfy the auditors, as already discussed earlier, that similar securities purchased in December, 1954 existed. The auditors were than to audit accounts of 1954 and not of 1955. In this connection reference may be made to <ORG>'s attitude to the auditors' surprise inspection on September 9, 1954, on the ground that they could not ask for inspection of securities purchased in 1955. It may also be mentioned that purchasing and selling securities was not really the business of <ORG>. <ORG> had to invest its money and, under the statutory requirements, had to invest a certain portion at least in <ORG> Securities. The value of <ORG> securities does not fluctuate much. <ORG> states, in answer to question No. 25 (under a. 342 Cr. P. C.): '<ORG> securities are gift edged securities and there is very small fluctuation in these.' The question of purchasing and selling of securities with a view-to profit could not therefore be the ordinary business of <ORG>. It has to purchase securities when the statutory requirements make it necessary, or when it has got funds which could be invested. <ORG> had <ORG> 3% Loan of 1957 in deposit with <ORG>, Bombay, the face value of the securities being Rs. 53,25,000, from April 6, 1951, onward. The fact that these securities remained intact for a period of over three years, bears out our view that the purchasing and selling of securities was not the normal business of <ORG>, Securities are purchased for investment and are redeemed on the date of maturity. In this connection, reference may be made to <NAME>'s statement in answer to question in cross-examination-The frequency of transactions relating to purchase and sale of securities depends upon the share market and its trends ? His answer was that was so, but that it also depended on the character of the company making the investment in securities. It may be said that the trend of the share market will only guide the purchase or sale transactions of securities of a company speculating in shares, like <ORG>, but will not affect the purchase and sale by a company whose business is not speculation of shares like <ORG>. <NAME> states that when on September 9, 1955, the auditors wanted the production of the securities, said to be at Bombay, in the next two days, he informed <ORG> about it and <ORG> said that he would arrange for their production after two days. <ORG>, however, took no steps to contact <NAME> at Bombay, but rang up <NAME> instead and asked him to certify the accounts as they had to be laid before the Company by September 30, and told him that everything was in order,. that he would give all satisfaction later, soon after <NAME> was available and that he did not ask for an extension of time for the filing of the accounts as that would affect the prestige of the company. On September 10, 1955, when <NAME> handed over the letter Exhibit P. 2 of even date from the auditors asking him to produce a statement of investments as on September 9, 1955, along with the securities or evidence if they were with other persons, by Tuesday, September 13, <ORG> had stated that <NAME>'s mother had died and that he would himself arrange for the inspection of securities direct with the auditors. <NAME>'s mother died on September 4, 1955. <ORG> had no reason to tell <NAME> on September 9 that the securities would be produced for inspection in the next two days, unless he believed that he could get them in that time on contacting <NAME>, or did not wish to tell him the real position. <ORG> states that he contacted <NAME> for the first time on September 15, the last day of the mourning and then learnt from <NAME> that the securities were not in existence, the money withdrawn for their purchase having been lent to <ORG>. The various statements made by <ORG> in these circumstances and his conduct go to show that he had a guilty mind and when he made the statement to <NAME> that the securities would be produced within two days, he trusted that he would be persuasive enough for the auditors to pass the accounts without further insistence on the production of those securities. <NAME>'s not going to Mr. <NAME>'s Office on September 16, and sending his relations to inform the latter of the shortfall in securities can have no other explanation than that he was guilty and therefore did not desire to have any direct talk about the matter with Mr. <NAME>. There was no need to avoid meeting him and miss the opportunity of explaining fully what <NAME> had done without his own knowledge. <NAME> has admitted that he sent his relations to Mr. <NAME> and has also admitted that what they) stated to Mr. <NAME> was under his instructions., He states in answer to question No. 450, that after the telephonic talk with <NAME> on the evening, of September 15, he consulted his brother Jai Dayal <NAME> and his son-in-law <NAME> about the position and about the action to be taken and that it was decided between them before they left for the office of Mr. <NAME> that they would tell him that either the securities would be restored or their price would be paid off as would be desired by the <ORG> and in answer to question No. 451, said that it was correct that these persons told Mr. <NAME> that a considerable amount of the securities were missing and that they were to make good the loss. It is clear that these persons decided not to disclose to Mr. <NAME> that the securities were not in stock because they were not actually purchased and the amount shown to be spent on them was lent to the Union Agencies. was not a case of the securities missing but a case of <ORG> not getting those securities at all. It is a reasonable inference from this conduct of <NAME> that he did not go himself to Mr. <NAME> as he was guilty and would have found it inconvenient to explain to him how the shortfall had taken place. We may now discuss the evidence relating to <NAME>'s making a confession to <NAME>. <NAME> was a Chartered Accountant and partner of <ORG> Chartered Accountants M/s. Khanna and <NAME>, New Delhi, and he was appointed by <ORG>, in exercise of its powers under s. 33(1) of the Insurance Act , 1938, on September 19, 1955, to investigate into the affairs of <ORG> company and to report to the <ORG> on such investigation. He started this work on September 20. <NAME>, having learnt from <NAME> about the missing of a number of <ORG> securities and the amount of their value from the statement prepared by him, called <NAME> to his office that evening in order to make a statement. <NAME> made the statements Exhibits P. 10 and P. 11. P. 10 reads : "'I have misappropriated securities of the order of Rs. 2,20,00,000 of <ORG> I have lost this money in speculation." Exhibit P. 11 reads: "Further stated on solemn affirmation. At any cost, I want to pay full amount by requesting my relatives or myself in the interest of the policy holders. " <NAME> admits having made the statement Exhibit P. 11. but made some inconsistent statements about his making the statement Exhibit P. 'LO. It is said that he never made that statement, but in certain circumstances he asked the Investigator to write what he considered proper and that he signed what <NAME> recorded. He was again administered oath and his further statement, Exhibit P. 11 was recorded. This was also read over and <NAME> signed it, admitting its accuracy. 362 <NAME> states that no threat or inducement or promise was offered to <NAME> before he made these statements. II His explanation for keeping <NAME> with him during the examination of <NAME> was that <NAME> had done the detailed auditing of the accounts of the company in pursuance of the firm <NAME> and <NAME> being appointed auditors for 1954 by <ORG>.
